lesson.title: The Network Core: A Mesh of Switches Moving Everyone's Data
lesson.summary: Defines the network core as the interconnected mesh of routers that forwards traffic between edges, and introduces packet switching and store and forward transmission as the mechanism that makes this possible.
lesson.body:
If the network edge is where hosts connect in, the network core is everything in between: a dense, interconnected mesh of routers, the switching nodes described earlier, linked together to move data between one edge and another. No single router in the core talks directly to every other router. Instead, data hops from router to router, each one making a local decision about where to send it next, until it eventually reaches the access link of the destination host. This mesh structure is deliberate: it means there are usually multiple possible paths between any two points, so if one router or link fails, traffic can often be rerouted around the problem rather than the whole network breaking.

The internet's network core works primarily through a technique called packet switching. Rather than reserving a dedicated path for an entire conversation the way an old telephone circuit did, data is broken into small chunks called packets, each labeled with its destination, and each router along the way forwards each packet independently based on that label. This means many different hosts' traffic can share the same links and routers, interleaved packet by packet, rather than each conversation needing its own reserved capacity. It is an efficient use of shared infrastructure, though it does mean packets belonging to the same conversation can occasionally take slightly different routes or arrive out of order.

Routers in the core generally use a method called store and forward: a router waits until it has received an entire packet before it starts sending that packet onward. This might sound like it wastes time, but it is what allows a router to check the packet, decide the best next hop, and forward it correctly. Each router essentially asks where this packet needs to go next, using information it maintains about the wider network, and then sends the packet out on the appropriate link toward the next router, and eventually toward the destination's edge.

Consider continuing the worked example from the previous section. Your request left your home router and entered your internet service provider's network core. From there, it likely hopped through several routers, each one examining the packet and forwarding it toward a router one step closer to the destination, until it reached the network edge on the other side, where the destination web server's access link finally delivered it. At no point did any single router in the core own the whole path, each one just made a local, independent forwarding decision, and the combination of all those decisions got the packet where it needed to go.

The network core's job is entirely about efficient, reliable forwarding at a massive scale, carrying the combined traffic of countless simultaneous conversations between edges. It has no interest in the content of any particular conversation, that job belongs entirely to the end systems at the edges, which is exactly the separation of concerns that lets the internet scale to the size it has.
